training-data.name: Training Data
training-data.bio: Podcast: A Model For Everyone: How Ronak From Trajectory Is Building Products For Continual Learning

html_en:
The Jensen Huang affair dominates tech Twitter while the AI industry quietly gets on with the more consequential work of building durable agents, smarter evals, and the infrastructure for models that never stop learning.

⚡ The Valley Rallies Around Jensen

The most viral moment in tech circles today wasn't a product launch — it was a petition. The "#StandWithJensen" movement swept through the AI builder community, with prominent voices lining up to defend NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang amid what many see as premature and unfair accusations in the press.

Amjad Masad of Replit was among the loudest voices, urging followers to "Read the Stand with Jensen letter and consider adding your name." When the petition site buckled under traffic, he stepped in personally:
Worked with the owner of the StandWithJensen page, which is built and hosted on Replit, to raise the rate limit. It should now scale! — @amasad

Garry Tan was equally direct: "Jensen deserves due process, not whatever is happening right now. I signed." Vercel's Guillermo Rauch simply co-signed.

Meanwhile, Peter Yang was doing actual journalism, pointing to the Singapore government's own statements as evidence that the WSJ's characterization of Alice Huang as a spy may have been a leap: "it's still unclear that Alice Huang is a spy despite WSJ jumping to conclusions." He encouraged readers to look at an account from an NVIDIA employee and do their own research — a refreshing note of epistemic humility in an otherwise hot-take-saturated news cycle.

🤖 Agents Grow Up: Durability, Commerce, and Real Infrastructure

While the drama played out in public, the quieter story of the day was serious agentic infrastructure coming online. Guillermo Rauch announced Workflow SDK 5 and Vercel Workflows in terms that signal a genuine step-change in reliability:

"The 'time to first step' and 'time between steps' have massively improved. We doubled down on encryption and security. The reliability of the overall system has been proven at massive scale. We've ironed out many subtle details and exercised many disaster-recovery scenarios." — @rauchg

He also teased that "Vercel Sandbox is inevitable" — a pointed hint at where code execution infrastructure is heading.

On the commerce side, Amjad Masad flagged an expanding partnership with Visa on agentic commerce, promising "more features and use cases coming" — a reminder that the payments layer for autonomous agents is being quietly assembled right now.

📊 The Benchmark Wars: Fatigue Sets In

Two independent data points today pushed back against the industry's obsession with leaderboard performance. Garry Tan shared results from his open source harness eval repo that cut through the hype around Fable 5.2:

"Keep Opus 5.5 as your coding default in Claude Code. On 52 coding tasks in Claude Code 2.1.322, Fable 5.2 solved about as many (82.7% vs 84.6%) but cost 2.80x as much per solved task." — @garrytan

Nikunj put it more bluntly:

"I thought after Llama 4 we had stopped benchmark-maxxing as a flex.. but it seems like the cartel is back again. There's no substitute to really using the models for your workflows to understand the best ones that actually work for your workflows." — @nikunj

Dan Shipper echoed the practical angle, noting why teams still pay for software even when frontier models can "vibe code" almost anything — real-world reliability and trust, not raw benchmark scores, remain the deciding factor.

🔬 The Continual Learning Frontier

The most thought-provoking content today came from the Training Data podcast, where Ronak from Trajectory laid out a quietly ambitious vision for a future where models never stop learning from production. His analogy is worth sitting with:

"When I was growing up, my family used to do road trips, and we would go to AAA and they would give us maps. If there's any point where we wanted to change our route, we'd have to call AAA or go to a physical location. I feel like that's the world we're in right now — we have these amazing agents, they're very intelligent, but anytime you want to update your course, you have to do an entire mass batch update. The final stage of continual learning is something more like Google Maps, where every single time you're driving, every route that you make, it is updating." — Ronak, Trajectory

He acknowledged the architectural challenges — Rich Sutton and David Silver have both argued that true continual learning isn't possible with today's transformer stacks — but pushed back gently, noting that models like DeepSeek are already incorporating "fast and slow memory within the weights" and skip connections that look a lot like early steps toward the goal. Watch/Listen: A Model For Everyone: How Ronak From Trajectory Is Building Products For Continual Learning

The product vision — unifying training, eval, and deployment into a single interface that any company can operate without a massive research team — is essentially a bet that fine-tuning and feedback loops will become as commoditized as cloud compute. Given how quickly the last five years have gone, that bet seems reasonable.

🩺 AI as a Lifeline

In what may be the most genuinely useful thing posted today, Peter Yang shared a free, open-source skill for cancer patients and their families that cuts through the noise of medical bureaucracy:

"If you know a loved one suffering from cancer or another long-term illness: Upload all of the patient's medical records to a Google Drive folder, tell ChatGPT or Claude to install my free /fuck-cancer skill, and point the skill at the folder to create a one-page brief, research clinical trials, and more." — @petergyang

The post drew 434 likes and counting — a small but telling sign of where the real appetite for AI utility lives. Not in benchmarks. Not in petitions. In someone, somewhere, getting a diagnosis explained clearly at 2am.
html_zh:
今天的AI圈有两条主线同时拉扯：一边是科技界为英伟达黄仁勋集体发声的罕见政治动员，另一边是模型评测的信任危机和智能体基础设施的悄然成熟。

🟥 #StandWithJensen：科技圈的一次罕见集结

本周最具话题性的事件，不是某个新模型发布，而是一场围绕英伟达CEO黄仁勋的舆论保卫战。针对《华尔街日报》对黄仁勋涉嫌出口管制违规的报道，科技界掀起了一场声势不小的联署运动。

Amjad Masad率先号召：

阅读《支持Jensen》公开信，考虑签上你的名字。#standwithjensen

Replit甚至直接介入基础设施层面——该联署页面本身就托管在Replit上，因流量激增触发限速，Masad随即与页面所有者合作提升了速率上限。Vercel联创Guillermo Rauch和YC掌门Garry Tan也相继联署，后者直言：

Jensen应当获得正当程序，而不是现在这种对待。

与此同时，Peter Yang援引新加坡政府资料，质疑WSJ报道中对Alice Huang"间谍"定性的草率，提醒读者自行核查。这场风波折射出：当AI芯片供应链与地缘政治深度交织，科技圈的政治神经已愈发敏感。

📊 基准测试的疲劳与真相

Fable 5.2发布后，围绕"它是否优于Claude Opus"的争论迅速升温。Garry Tan用自己的开源评测框架给出了一个冷静的答案：

在Claude Code 2.1.322的52个编程任务中，Fable 5.2解决了约82.7%，Opus解决了84.6%，但Fable每个解决任务的成本高出2.80倍。继续把Opus 5.5作为Claude Code的编程默认模型吧。

他的开源评测仓库也随之公开。Nikunj则更加犀利：

我以为Llama 4之后我们已经停止把刷榜当作炫耀手段……但卡特尔似乎又回来了。没有什么能替代真正把模型用于你自己工作流程的体验。现实是，真正重要的基准寥寥无几，懂的人自然懂。其余的基本上是摆姿态，或者只是爬一座山再把它当营销用。

Dan Shipper也从另一角度回答了"为什么团队即使在AI能生成一切的时代仍然为软件付费"这个问题——答案指向的，依然是可靠性与工作流契合度，而非原始能力。

🤖 智能体基础设施：从概念到工程

安静却重要的一天。Guillermo Rauch宣布Workflow SDK 5与Vercel Workflows正式推出：

这是智能体领域的一个重要里程碑。"第一步的响应时间"与"步骤间时延"大幅改善；我们在加密与安全上加倍投入；整体系统的可靠性已在大规模场景下得到验证。底层持久化日志现已可供任何智能体框架复用——durable-harness由此诞生。

在商业侧，Amjad Masad透露Replit与Visa在智能体商务领域的合作正在深化，更多功能即将推出——这或许是"AI代替人类刷卡购物"这一愿景离现实最近的一次。

🔁 持续学习：从AAA地图到Google Maps

本日最值得细读的内容来自播客 Training Data。Watch/Listen: A Model For Everyone: How Ronak From Trajectory Is Building Products For Continual Learning

Trajectory创始人Ronak用一个极具画面感的比喻，解释了当前AI系统与真正"持续学习"之间的鸿沟：

我们小时候家里会去AAA拿一堆地图，出发前规划好路线。如果途中想改路线，只能打电话或跑到实体门店。我觉得这就是我们现在所处的世界——有很聪明的智能体，但每次想更新，都只能做一次大规模的批量更新。真正的持续学习应该像Google Maps：每一次驾驶，每一条路线，它都在实时更新，聚合学习最快路径和拥堵位置。那才是我想抵达的世界。

他也坦承现实的艰难：在Windsurf时，训练一个前沿模型需要六到九个月、数亿美元的算力与研发投入，以及庞大的研究团队。Trajectory的赌注，是把这套流程产品化，让每家公司都能触达。

❤️ 用AI对抗癌症

最后，一个小而有力的信号。Peter Yang发布了一个名为 /fuck-cancer 的免费技能工具，可让ChatGPT或Claude读取患者全部医疗记录、生成一页摘要、检索临床试验。他写道：

用AI的全部力量来对抗糟糕的疾病。

这条推文获得了今日原始数据中最高的互动量之一（434赞、36转推）。在所有关于基准和联署的喧嚣之外，这或许才是AI真正值得被记住的用途。
